## Design

### 2026-10-10 – Week 1 – Designing My First Custom PCB

**8h**

Week 1 – Designing My First Custom PCB
During this session, I worked on designing and finishing my first custom PCB in KiCad. I started by building the schematic and connecting all of the components, including the XIAO ESP32-C3, DHT11 sensor, OLED display, buttons, resistor, and the connector for the MPU6050.
After finishing the schematic, I assigned the correct footprints to each component and transferred everything into the PCB Editor. One of the most challenging parts was arranging the components and routing all of the connections without creating conflicts. I had to move several components and redo some traces multiple times until everything could be connected correctly.
I also wanted the PCB to feel like my own project instead of simply copying the example from the guide. I created a custom spaceship-shaped board outline inspired by the LUNARIS-01, a spaceship from another project I am working on. I also added LUNARIS-01 text and custom space-themed silkscreen artwork with a planet and rings.
After routing the board, I ran KiCad's Design Rules Checker. The board showed 0 unconnected items. The remaining two courtyard errors came from the imported display footprint and are the same errors shown as acceptable in the Starbie guide. I also checked that adding the custom silkscreen artwork did not introduce any new errors.
This session taught me a lot about how a schematic becomes a physical PCB, how footprints and routing work, and how PCB layout sometimes requires reorganizing components instead of trying to force traces through a bad layout. It was challenging, especially since this was my first time doing this, but by the end of the session I had a routed and customized PCB that I was happy with.

### 2026-10-11 – October 11: Firmware, manufacturing files, and BOM!

**5.75h**

October 11: Firmware, manufacturing files, and BOM!
Today I continued working on my Starbie project after finishing the PCB design and posting my reel. Most of today's work was focused on customizing the firmware, preparing the PCB for manufacturing, and finishing the bill of materials.
I started by working on the Starbie firmware in Arduino IDE. Instead of keeping the default pet, I wanted to make the project feel more connected to the LUNARIS-01 theme, so I created my own 32x32 pet called NOVA and replaced the original sprite with it. I also added a small animated star effect that appears next to NOVA.
After that, I experimented with the MPU6050 controls and added a hidden easter egg. If the user performs a specific sequence of movements (up, down, right, left, and then a shake), a secret character called Cubito appears on the OLED for a few seconds. Getting the sequence detection to work in the code was one of the more complicated parts because I needed to make sure each movement was registered separately and that the normal shake behavior still worked.
I compiled the firmware several times while making these changes. The final version compiled successfully with no errors. I cannot physically test the firmware yet because I do not have the assembled PCB, so for now I have only verified that the code compiles correctly.
Once the firmware was finished, I prepared the manufacturing files in KiCad. I exported the copper, solder mask, silkscreen, and Edge.Cuts Gerber layers, as well as separate PTH and NPTH drill files. I checked the generated files, placed them together in a ZIP called LUNARIS-01-Gerbers.zip, and uploaded the ZIP to my GitHub repository.
Finally, I worked on the bill of materials for the project. I found real vendors and prices for the XIAO ESP32-C3, DHT11 sensor, 0.96" OLED display, MPU6050, two Cherry MX switches, and the 10kΩ resistor. I also tried to balance component quality with the $30 Tier 1 budget instead of simply choosing the cheapest parts. The current parts total is $22.44, leaving some room in the budget for other costs.
Today taught me a lot about the steps between designing a PCB and actually being ready to manufacture and build it. I also learned more about writing firmware around physical gestures and state, exporting manufacturing files correctly, and planning a realistic BOM around a limited budget.
Time spent: approximately 5 hours 45 minutes.

### 2026-10-11 – I continued researching the remaining components for my project, comparing prices, compatibility, and vendors while making sure the complete parts list stayed within the Tier 1 budget.

**1h**

I continued researching the remaining components for my project, comparing prices, compatibility, and vendors while making sure the complete parts list stayed within the Tier 1 budget.
After finishing the bill of materials in Half Life, I noticed that the repository checker recommended including a BOM as a CSV file as well. I organized the components, quantities, prices, vendors, descriptions, and product links into a BOM.csv file. I verified that the parts total matched my BOM in Half Life at $22.44, then uploaded the CSV to my GitHub repository so the project has a separate and easy-to-read parts list.
This process also helped me understand why keeping a structured BOM is useful when moving from designing a PCB to eventually ordering the components and building the hardware.
